subtitle: Turning bits into voltages, marking where frames start and end, and noticing, or fixing, the bit that got flipped.

encoding.body:
A wire carries voltages, not ones and zeros, so bits must be mapped to levels, and you get to choose how. The simplest plan is NRZ-L: hold a level for the whole bit. NRZ-I flips level for a 1. Both have a problem: they lose the clock on long runs of identical bits, so the receiver forgets when one bit ends and the next begins.

Manchester fixes this by putting a transition in the middle of every bit (low→high for 1, high→low for 0). The receiver recovers the clock at the cost of double the signal rate, and it was the code of classic 10 Mb/s Ethernet. Bipolar AMI sends 0 as no pulse and alternates + and − for 1s. Step through the figure and see each code turn the same bits into a different waveform. Why does Manchester help the receiver? Because every bit carries a transition it can lock onto.
keynotes: NRZ-L holds a level for the whole bit and NRZ-I flips level for a 1; both lose the clock on long runs of identical bits.
Manchester puts a transition in the middle of every bit (low→high for 1, high→low for 0), so the receiver recovers the clock, at the cost of double the signal rate.
Bipolar AMI sends 0 as no pulse and alternates + and − for 1s.

framing.body:
Bits arrive in an endless stream. How does the receiver know where one frame stops and the next begins? You need a marker. With a special marker, a flag byte (HDLC uses 01111110). But what if the data itself happens to contain the flag? The trick is called bit stuffing: after five consecutive 1s in the data, the sender inserts a 0, which the receiver removes.

See it with the data 0111111011, which contains six 1s in a row. After the first five 1s insert a 0, so the flag pattern 01111110 cannot appear inside the data: 0111110 11011 . HDLC inserts a 0 after five consecutive 1s.
keynotes: A flag byte marks where a frame starts and ends; HDLC uses 01111110.
Bit stuffing inserts a 0 after five consecutive 1s in the data, and the receiver removes it.
This stops the flag pattern appearing inside the data.

crc.body:
Noise flips bits, and you need to notice. Three tools, from simple to strong. A single parity bit catches any odd number of flipped bits but no even number. The checksum adds the words and sends the complement. The CRC treats the message as a polynomial and sends the remainder of dividing by an agreed generator G(x): the receiver divides the whole frame and accepts only a zero remainder.

It catches all single-bit errors, all bursts up to the generator’s degree, and almost everything else. Dividing 1101011011 by 10011 gives the CRC 1110; the frame sent is 11010110111110. The division is long division with XOR, no carries. In the second figure a bit flips in transit, and the receiver’s remainder is not zero. A non-zero remainder means the frame was corrupted.
keynotes: A single parity bit catches any odd number of flipped bits but no even number; the checksum adds the words and sends the complement.
The CRC sends the remainder of dividing the message by a generator G(x); the receiver accepts only a zero remainder.
Dividing 1101011011 by 10011 gives CRC 1110, and the frame sent is 11010110111110.

hamming.body:
Detection means asking for a retransmission. What if the receiver could fix the error itself? Hamming codes do exactly this for a single-bit error. Parity bits sit at positions 1, 2, 4, 8…; parity bit p covers every position whose binary index contains p. After an error the failing parity checks, read as a binary number, give the position of the bad bit: the syndrome.

Data 1011 encodes to 0110011; corrupt bit 5 and the syndrome reads 5. How many parity bits do you need? 4 data bits need r parity bits with 2ʳ ≥ 4 + r + 1, and 2³ = 8 ≥ 4 + 3 + 1, so Hamming(7,4): 7 bits sent for 4 data bits. If the syndrome is 101 in binary, bit 5 is wrong.
keynotes: Hamming codes let the receiver correct a single-bit error itself.
Parity bits sit at positions 1, 2, 4, 8…; the failing parity checks read as a binary number give the position of the bad bit, the syndrome.
Data 1011 encodes to 0110011, and Hamming(7,4) sends 7 bits for 4 data bits.

protocols.body:
Now see how these ideas appear in real protocols. HDLC and PPP frame point-to-point links with flags, an address/control field, a payload and a CRC. Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) frames carry destination and source MAC (6 bytes each), a type, 46–1500 bytes of data and a 4-byte CRC.

You can think of the data link layer as having two sub-layers: LLC (flow and error control, protocol multiplexing) and MAC (who may transmit, and addressing). The maximum Ethernet payload is 1500 bytes.
keynotes: HDLC and PPP frame point-to-point links with flags, an address/control field, a payload and a CRC.
Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) frames carry destination and source MAC (6 bytes each), a type, 46–1500 bytes of data and a 4-byte CRC.
The data link layer splits into LLC (flow and error control, protocol multiplexing) and MAC (who may transmit, and addressing).

summary.body:
Three lines to keep.

  • Line coding maps bits to signals; Manchester embeds the clock.
  • Framing needs flags and bit stuffing.
  • CRC detects, Hamming corrects single errors.
keynotes: Line coding maps bits to signals, and Manchester embeds the clock.
Framing needs flags and bit stuffing.
CRC detects errors and Hamming corrects single errors.
